etymology: From Latin perpetuus, continuous, unbroken, from per (through) and petere (to go toward). Webster 1828: never ceasing; continuing forever in future time; unfailing. In the Authorized Version perpetual renders Hebrew words of unbroken continuance, and it is applied to statutes, to covenants, to the fire on the altar — and, once, with terrible irony, to backsliding.
biblical_def: Perpetual in Scripture describes what does not stop, and its most frequent home is the law of the sanctuary. The sabbath is kept throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant (Exodus 31:16). The dietary boundary is set as a perpetual statute for your generations throughout all your dwellings (Leviticus 3:17). The fire on the altar was never to go out. In each case the word does two things at once: it binds Israel across time, and it testifies that the God who commanded is Himself unchanging. Jeremiah then carries the term into the promise of the new covenant, where it becomes gospel rather than regulation: Come, and let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten (Jeremiah 50:5). The unbrokenness has moved from the observance to the LORD who keeps it, which is precisely the difference between the two covenants. And the same prophet turns the word against his people with devastating precision: Why then is this people of Jerusalem slidden back by a perpetual backsliding? (Jeremiah 8:5). Man is capable of perpetuity too. Left to himself he is unbroken in only one direction, and that verse names it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PERPETUAL as never ceasing; continuing forever in future time; destined to be eternal; unfailing; everlasting; also, continued without intermission, and permanent as opposed to temporary.
webster_full: PERPETUAL, a. [L. perpetuus, from perpes, perpetis.] — Never ceasing; continuing forever in future time; destined to be eternal; as a perpetual covenant. Continuing without intermission; uninterrupted; as a perpetual stream. Permanent; fixed; not temporary.

Webster’s two senses — forever in future time and without intermission — are both needed. A perpetual statute binds every generation; a perpetual fire is never allowed to die on any single night. Israel had to obey the word in both directions at once, which is why the priesthood was staffed around the clock.
scriptures: Exodus 31:16
Wherefore the children of Israel shall keep the sabbath, to observe the sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant.
Leviticus 3:17
It shall be a perpetual statute for your generations throughout all your dwellings, that ye eat neither fat nor blood.
Jeremiah 50:5
They shall ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward, saying, Come, and let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten.
Jeremiah 8:5
Why then is this people of Jerusalem slidden back by a perpetual backsliding? they hold fast deceit, they refuse to return.
Leviticus 6:13
The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out.
corruption_summary: Perpetual is corrupted when the perpetuity of Israel’s ceremonial statutes is used either to bind the church to abrogated ceremonies, or, in the opposite error, to argue that God’s promises expire because His ceremonies did.
corruption_paragraphs: Because the Authorized Version calls the ceremonial statutes perpetual, two contrary errors have grown from the word. The first insists that whatever God called perpetual must still bind, and so reinstates dietary law, the seventh-day sabbath as ceremony, or a standing sacrificial calendar. The Reformed answer distinguishes the moral, ceremonial, and judicial law: the moral law abides because it reflects God’s character; the ceremonial was perpetual for the age it governed and is fulfilled and therefore ended in Christ, which is Hebrews’ entire argument. A shadow is not abolished when the body arrives — it is answered. The fire on the altar was to burn without going out, and it does not burn now, because the offering it served has been made once for all.

The second error runs the other way and is more damaging. Observing that God’s perpetual ceremonies did in fact cease, it concludes that His covenant language is loose, and that promises to His people may likewise lapse. Jeremiah forecloses this. The perpetual covenant he announces is one that shall not be forgotten, and its unbrokenness rests on the LORD rather than on Israel’s observance — which is exactly why it holds where the first covenant did not. God’s faithfulness is the constant; the administration changes. And Jeremiah 8:5 supplies the sober counterweight, because perpetual backsliding is a real human capacity. Unbroken continuance is not automatically a virtue. Everything depends on the direction of the line.
roots_summary: Two Hebrew words carry perpetual. One means the age-long stretch of time; the other means continual, regular, without a gap. The first governs covenants, the second governs the daily service — and the difference explains why some perpetual things ceased and others did not.
roots_lines: Hebrew ōlām (H5769) — long duration, antiquity, futurity; the age-long word rendered perpetual, everlasting, and for ever (Exodus 31:16; Leviticus 3:17).
Hebrew tāmīd (H8548) — continual, regular, uninterrupted; the word behind the daily burnt offering and the fire that never went out (Leviticus 6:13).
The word ōlām measures the span of an age and takes its length from the thing it modifies; applied to God it is absolute, applied to a ceremony it runs to that ceremony’s fulfilment.
Hebrew āvōn (H5771) — iniquity, guilt; the condition Jeremiah 8:5 diagnoses as perpetual backsliding, where man’s own continuance runs the wrong way.
usage: A perpetual statute for your generations (Leviticus 3:17) binds an age, not every age — the shadow ends when the body comes.
Jeremiah’s perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten (Jeremiah 50:5) rests its unbrokenness on the LORD, not on the observer.
A perpetual backsliding (Jeremiah 8:5): man is capable of unbroken continuance too, and by nature only in one direction.

etymology: Old English wundorfull, full of wonder. Webster 1828: adapted to excite wonder or admiration; strange; astonishing. The modern collapse of the word into a mild compliment is recent; in the Authorized Version wonderful means what exceeds comprehension, and in Isaiah 9:6 it is not a description of the Child but one of His names.
biblical_def: Wonderful in Scripture marks the boundary of the creature’s understanding. It is not praise for something pleasant; it names what cannot be taken in. David uses it of God’s knowledge of him: Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it (Psalm 139:6). Job, silenced at last, uses the same word of God’s works: things too wonderful for me, which I knew not (Job 42:3). Agur lists what he cannot trace: There be three things which are too wonderful for me (Proverbs 30:18). In every case the word measures a limit, and the man who uses it is confessing that he has reached his. Then Isaiah takes that limit-word and makes it a proper name: his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). The Child born to us is Himself the incomprehensible thing. He is not merely wonderful in His deeds; He bears the name. And the Authorized Version keeps the word in the Gospels for what men saw Him do — the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful things that he did (Matthew 21:15) — where the wonders provoked not worship but displeasure, which is its own commentary on the fallen heart.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WONDERFUL as adapted to excite wonder or admiration; strange; astonishing; and, as an adverb in older usage, wonderfully. Webster ties it directly to wonder, the emotion excited by novelty or by something that exceeds the power of comprehension.
webster_full: WONDERFUL, a. — Adapted to excite wonder or admiration; strange; astonishing; as a wonderful prospect. Wonder, n. — That emotion which is excited by novelty, or the presentation to the sight or mind of something new, unusual, strange, great, extraordinary, or not well understood.

Webster’s definition of wonder is the key: not well understood. The word belongs to the limits of the mind. Two centuries of using it for weather and weekends have worn that away, so that a modern reader meets Isaiah 9:6 and hears a compliment where the prophet wrote a name.
scriptures: Isaiah 9:6

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
Psalm 139:6
Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.
Job 42:3
Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge? therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not.
Proverbs 30:18
There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not:
Matthew 21:15
And when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying in the temple, and saying, Hosanna to the Son of David; they were sore displeased,
corruption_summary: Wonderful has been worn down from a word marking the limit of human comprehension into a mild term of approval, so that the titles of Isaiah 9:6 now read as warmth rather than as a claim to deity.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is linguistic before it is doctrinal, and it is nearly complete. A word that once meant exceeding the power of comprehension is now spent on meals and holidays. The cost is paid at Isaiah 9:6, where a modern ear hears a string of affectionate epithets for a beloved figure. The prophet is doing something else entirely: he is naming a child The mighty God and The everlasting Father, and Wonderful stands at the head of that list as the confession that the One so named cannot be comprehended by those naming Him. Read as a compliment, the verse becomes sentimental. Read as it stands, it is one of the plainest declarations of the deity of Christ in the Old Testament, and the Christmas card usage quietly disarms it.

There is a second and quieter loss. The three men who use the word of their own limits — David, Job, Agur — are all mature believers, and each is describing something about God he cannot reach. That posture has largely disappeared. A theology that has an answer for everything has ceased to find anything too wonderful for it, and a piety with no room for incomprehensibility will eventually shrink God to the size of its explanations. The Reformed tradition guarded this deliberately with the doctrine of divine incomprehensibility: God is truly known, because He has revealed Himself, and never exhaustively known, because He is God. Job’s confession is not a failure of theology. It is the end of it, and the beginning of worship.
roots_summary: The Hebrew behind wonderful is a single root meaning to be extraordinary, beyond reach, surpassing. It is the same root that supplies the noun for miracle, which is why the word never means merely pleasant — a wonder is something only God can do.
roots_lines: Hebrew pele (H6382) — a wonder, a marvel, an extraordinary thing; the noun standing as the name in Isaiah 9:6, his name shall be called Wonderful.
The same root gives the verb rendered too wonderful in Psalm 139:6, Job 42:3, and Proverbs 30:18 — literally, too surpassing, out of reach.
In the Old Testament the noun is used almost exclusively of God’s acts; when Isaiah applies it as a personal name, the transfer from deed to Person is the point of the verse.
Greek thaumasios — wonderful, marvellous (Matthew 21:15, the wonderful things that he did). Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.
usage: Too wonderful for me (Psalm 139:6; Job 42:3; Proverbs 30:18) is a confession of limit, spoken three times by mature men.
In Isaiah 9:6 Wonderful is a name, not an adjective — the Child is the incomprehensible thing.
The chief priests saw the wonderful things that he did and were sore displeased (Matthew 21:15); wonders do not produce faith.

etymology: Old English dung, manure. Webster 1828: the excrement of animals. The Authorized Version uses the word without flinching, and its translators chose it deliberately in Philippians 3:8, where the Greek is a coarse term for refuse. Scripture’s realism about filth is part of its doctrine of holiness.
biblical_def: Dung is Scripture’s blunt word for what must be carried outside, and it is used with theological precision. In the sin offering, the parts that bore the guilt were removed from the camp entire: the bullock for the sin offering, and the goat for the sin offering, whose blood was brought in to make atonement in the holy place, shall one carry forth without the camp; and they shall burn in the fire their skins, and their flesh, and their dung (Leviticus 16:27). Nothing of the sin-bearer stayed inside. Hebrews reads that ritual as pointing to Christ suffering without the gate. The prophets use the word for the shame of judgment — the unburied dead lie for dung upon the face of the earth (Jeremiah 8:2) — and Malachi turns it on corrupt priests with shocking directness: I will spread dung upon your faces, even the dung of your solemn feasts (Malachi 2:3). The offerings they profaned become the filth that marks them. Then Paul, listing his pedigree, circumcision, tribe, blamelessness under law, weighs it all and reaches for the same category: I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord... and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ (Philippians 3:8). Not worthless things — his best things, and he calls them refuse beside Christ.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DUNG as the excrement of animals; and as a verb, to manure with dung, or to enrich land. Webster also records the compound uses the Authorized Version knows: dunghill, dung-gate, dung-port.
webster_full: DUNG, n. — The excrement of animals. DUNG, v.t. — To manure with dung; to enrich land by spreading dung upon it.

Webster notes the agricultural use, and Scripture assumes it too — the fig tree in the parable is dunged in the hope of fruit. But the Authorized Version’s theological uses are all removal, not enrichment: dung goes outside the camp, outside the gate, off the altar. Where the word appears in the sanctuary it marks what may not remain.
scriptures: Philippians 3:8

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
Leviticus 16:27

And the bullock for the sin offering, and the goat for the sin offering, whose blood was brought in to make atonement in the holy place, shall one carry forth without the camp; and they shall burn in the fire their skins, and their flesh, and their dung.
Malachi 2:3
Behold, I will corrupt your seed, and spread dung upon your faces, even the dung of your solemn feasts; and one shall take you away with it.
Jeremiah 8:2

And they shall spread them before the sun, and the moon, and all the host of heaven, whom they have loved, and whom they have served, and after whom they have walked, and whom they have sought, and whom they have worshipped: they shall not be gathered, nor be buried; they shall be for dung upon the face of the earth.
corruption_summary: Dung is corrupted mainly by softening — modern renderings and modern preaching blunt Philippians 3:8 into rubbish or garbage, which loses Paul’s deliberate coarseness and, with it, the violence of the comparison he is making.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul chose a crude word on purpose, and the Authorized Version translated it honestly. The refinement of dung into rubbish is not merely a matter of taste; it changes the argument. Rubbish is neutral waste, discarded without feeling. Dung is offensive, and it is offensive precisely because it was once food. Paul’s list is not of sins he abandoned but of genuine advantages — covenant circumcision, the tribe of Benjamin, the law’s blamelessness — the very things a devout man would count as gain. He says that beside Christ these become excrement. The doctrine of justification requires that violence. Self-righteousness is not merely insufficient; it is filthy, and Isaiah had already said as much of our righteousnesses. A translation that spares the reader spares him the doctrine.

The second misuse runs opposite, and it appears wherever Philippians 3 is read as contempt for God’s good gifts. Paul is not despising circumcision, the law, or his people; he defends all three elsewhere at length. The word is comparative and situational: these things are dung that I may win Christ. Held as gain over against Christ, a lawful advantage becomes refuse; held under Christ, it is honoured. Leviticus 16:27 makes the same point ritually — what is carried outside the camp is not garbage swept from the floor but the sin offering itself, the holiest animal in the service, bearing what cannot be allowed to remain. The category is not worthless. It is must go outside.
roots_summary: Several Hebrew nouns for refuse and animal waste lie behind the Old Testament’s dung, and one blunt Greek noun behind Paul’s. The consistent thread is not disgust for its own sake but exclusion — what belongs outside the camp.
roots_lines: Greek skubalon — refuse, offal, dung; what is thrown to the dogs (Philippians 3:8). A deliberately coarse word, and the Authorized Version renders it plainly. Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.
Hebrew gelēl (H1557) — dung, a dung ball; the root also underlies the contemptuous word the prophets use for idols.
Hebrew peresh — the offal of a sacrificial animal, carried outside the camp with the skin and flesh (Leviticus 16:27). Untagged in this lexicon.
That the prophets’ word for idols shares a root with dung is not accidental; Ezekiel in particular uses it as a standing insult to what Israel worshipped.
usage: The sin offering was burnt without the camp, skin, flesh and dung together (Leviticus 16:27) — the sin-bearer goes entirely outside.
Malachi threatens corrupt priests with the dung of your solemn feasts (Malachi 2:3): their own offerings become their disgrace.
Paul counts his best credentials but dung, that I may win Christ (Philippians 3:8). The word is coarse on purpose.

etymology: From Latin persuadere, from per (thoroughly) and suadere (to advise, to urge). Webster 1828: influenced by argument or reason; convinced. In the Authorized Version the passive is the significant form — men are persuaded, and the New Testament’s vocabulary of assurance, obedience, and faith all grow from the same Greek root.
biblical_def: To be persuaded in the New Testament is to have been brought to settled conviction, and Paul uses the word at exactly the points where his confidence is most exposed. Facing every conceivable threat he writes, For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come (Romans 8:38) shall separate us from the love of God. In a Roman prison, awaiting execution, he says, I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day (2 Timothy 1:12) — the persuasion rests not on his own endurance but on Another’s ability. Of Abraham he says the same thing in the same word: being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform (Romans 4:21). In every instance the object of persuasion is God’s power to keep His word, not the believer’s power to keep his footing. That is the Reformed doctrine of assurance in a participle. And the Lord’s own verdict marks the limit of evidence: If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead (Luke 16:31). Persuasion is not manufactured by spectacle. It is worked by the Word and the Spirit.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PERSUADE as to influence by argument, advice, entreaty or expostulation; to draw or incline the will to a determination; and PERSUADED as convinced, influenced by argument or reason.
webster_full: PERSUADE, v.t. [L. persuadeo; per and suadeo, to advise or incite.] — To influence by argument, advice, intreaty or expostulation; to draw or incline the will to a determination. To convince; to satisfy the mind by evidence. PERSUADED, pp. — Influenced or drawn to an opinion or determination; convinced.

Webster’s phrase to draw or incline the will is precise and important. Persuasion in the older sense does not merely furnish the mind with information; it moves the will. That is why the same Greek root gives the New Testament its words for faith, for obedience, and for confidence — a man who is persuaded has been moved, not merely informed.
scriptures: Romans 8:38
For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come,
2 Timothy 1:12

For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.
Romans 4:21
And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform.
Luke 16:31
And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.
Hebrews 11:6
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
corruption_summary: Persuaded is corrupted when assurance is relocated from the character and power of God to the intensity of the believer’s own conviction — so that a man examines how persuaded he feels rather than Who has promised.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage has thinned persuaded into strongly of the opinion, and the pastoral damage shows up immediately in the matter of assurance. If being persuaded is a state of feeling, then assurance rises and falls with the weather of the soul, and the anxious believer is driven to measure his own certainty — which is the surest way to lose it. Every one of Paul’s uses points the other direction. He is persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him. The object is God’s ability. Abraham was fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform. Again the object is God’s ability. Assurance in the Reformed confessions is founded on the divine promises, the inward evidence of graces, and the witness of the Spirit — and the first of those three is first for this reason.

The second corruption is the evidentialist one, and Luke 16:31 was written against it. A widespread assumption holds that unbelief would yield to a sufficiently spectacular demonstration — that if a man came back from the dead, the matter would be settled. Christ says otherwise, and He says it in a parable told shortly before a man named Lazarus was in fact raised, after which the response of the authorities was to plot to kill him too. Persuasion is not produced by escalating evidence, because unbelief is not fundamentally an evidential problem. It is a matter of the will, which is why Scripture pairs this word with the will and not merely the mind, and why the ordinary means — Moses and the prophets, the preached Word — remain the instrument God actually uses.
roots_summary: One Greek root supplies this whole family. From peithō, to persuade, come the New Testament’s words for faith, for obedience, and for confident assurance — which is a theology in an etymology.
roots_lines: Greek peithō (G3982) — to persuade, to convince; in the passive and perfect, to be persuaded, to trust, to have confidence (Romans 8:38; 2 Timothy 1:12; Luke 16:31).
Greek plērophoreō (G4135) — to fill completely, to fully assure; the word behind fully persuaded (Romans 4:21).
Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, trust; built on the same root as peithō. Faith in the New Testament is a persuaded condition, not a leap in the dark.
Hebrew āman (H539) — to confirm, to support, to believe; the Old Testament counterpart, and the root of Amen. To believe is to lean one’s weight on what holds.
usage: I am persuaded (Romans 8:38) introduces a list of every power that might separate the believer — and dismisses them all.
Persuaded that he is able (2 Timothy 1:12): the object of assurance is God’s ability, never the believer’s intensity.
Neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead (Luke 16:31) — unbelief is not cured by escalating evidence.

etymology: Old English scearp, cutting, keen. Webster 1828: having a very thin edge or fine point; keen; piercing; also severe, harsh, biting. In the Authorized Version the word belongs overwhelmingly to two things — swords and tongues — and Scripture repeatedly puts them in the same sentence.
biblical_def: Sharp in Scripture is a word about edges, and its most sustained use joins the edge of a blade to the edge of speech. Isaiah’s Servant is equipped as a weapon: he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me (Isaiah 49:2). The risen Christ appears with the same figure made literal: out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword (Revelation 1:16). The image is not decorative. It says the Lord’s conquest is accomplished by speech, and that His word is an instrument that cuts. Hebrews makes the claim explicit and turns it on the reader: the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart (Hebrews 4:12). Scripture is not primarily the object of the reader’s examination; it is the instrument of his. But the same edge exists in fallen mouths, and David names it: the wicked are those whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword (Psalm 57:4). Luke even records sharpness among the apostles — the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder (Acts 15:39). The faculty is the same. Only the hand differs.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SHARP as having a very thin edge or fine point; keen; acute; piercing; severe; also, eager, quick of perception, and biting in speech. Webster gives both the physical and the verbal sense under one head.
webster_full: SHARP, a. [Sax. scearp.] — Having a very thin edge or fine point; keen; acute; not blunt. Piercing; penetrating; as a sharp wind. Severe; harsh; biting; sarcastic; as sharp words. Eager; keen; quick, as of appetite or perception.

Webster runs the blade sense and the speech sense together without apology, exactly as the Authorized Version does. A sharp word and a sharp sword are one metaphor in English because they are one metaphor in Scripture, and the reason is given in Hebrews 4:12: God’s speech actually cuts.
scriptures: Hebrews 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
Revelation 1:16
And he had in his right hand seven stars: and out of his mouth went a sharp twoedged sword: and his countenance was as the sun shineth in his strength.
Isaiah 49:2
And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me;
Psalm 57:4
My soul is among lions: and I lie even among them that are set on fire, even the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword.
Acts 15:39
And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus;
corruption_summary: Sharp is corrupted when the sharpness Scripture assigns to God’s word is claimed for the preacher’s manner — harshness mistaken for faithfulness — and, in the opposite direction, when the edge is filed off the Word itself so that it may no longer wound before it heals.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption flatters the severe. Hebrews 4:12 says the word of God is sharper than any twoedged sword; it does not say the preacher should be. Men who have confused the two produce a ministry that cuts by temperament rather than by text, and then reads the resulting damage as evidence of faithfulness. Acts 15:39 is the standing rebuke: sharpness between brethren is recorded in Scripture without approval, and it separated Paul from Barnabas. Psalm 57:4 puts a sharp tongue squarely among the weapons of the wicked. The edge belongs to the Word. The minister’s calling is to hold it steadily and get out of its way, and Paul’s own instruction is that the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men.

The second corruption is now more common and does more damage. Preaching that has decided in advance never to wound must blunt the instrument, and a blunt sword does not divide soul and spirit or discern the thoughts and intents of the heart — it merely rests on the surface. Where the whole counsel of God is filtered for what will not offend, the hearer is protected from the only thing that could save him. Scripture assumes the wound is the beginning of the healing; the Spirit uses a cutting word to convict before He uses a binding word to comfort. A ministry that removes the first has not become kinder. It has become useless, and it has quietly asserted an authority over the Word that no man has.
roots_summary: The Hebrew and Greek behind sharp are ordinary adjectives of keenness, and their theological weight comes from the nouns they modify. In the Authorized Version those nouns are almost always a sword or a mouth.
roots_lines: Hebrew chad — sharp, keen (Isaiah 49:2; Psalm 57:4). Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.
Hebrew cherev (H2719) — sword; the noun that sharp most often modifies, and the standing image of both warfare and judgment.
Greek machaira (G3162) — a sword or dagger; the word Paul uses for the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
Greek tomoteros — sharper, more cutting; the comparative in Hebrews 4:12, from a root meaning to cut. Untagged in this lexicon.
usage: The word of God is sharper than any twoedged sword (Hebrews 4:12) — the edge belongs to the text, not the temperament.
The Servant’s mouth like a sharp sword (Isaiah 49:2) and Christ’s sharp twoedged sword (Revelation 1:16): the conquest is by speech.
A sharp tongue sits among the weapons of the wicked (Psalm 57:4), and sharp contention divided Paul from Barnabas (Acts 15:39).
